mcqs.question: A 50-column table has one upstream column change. Why does column-level lineage give a more actionable answer than table-level lineage here?
options: Table-level lineage cannot be automated, so it's always slower to check regardless of scope
Column-level lineage costs nothing extra to build compared to table-level lineage
Table-level lineage doesn't exist for tables with more than 10 columns

Table-level lineage would flag every downstream consumer of the whole table, while column-level lineage narrows it to only the specific columns actually affected by the change, out of potentially many unrelated ones
mcqs.explanation: The value of column-level granularity is precision — it distinguishes "this whole table matters" from "this one specific column matters," which shrinks the investigation dramatically when only a fraction of the table's columns are actually affected. Table-level lineage is fully automatable and has no column-count limit; the real trade-off is that column-level tracking costs more effort to build and maintain, not that it's free.

mcqs.question: Before changing a widely-used column, an engineer wants to know exactly which downstream consumers would be affected. What does lineage provide that informally asking around doesn't?
options: Lineage guarantees the change itself will not cause any issues
A reliable, traceable graph traversal that surfaces every reachable downstream consumer, rather than relying on people remembering and volunteering that information
Lineage replaces the need for a data contract entirely
Asking around is always faster and more complete than checking a lineage graph
mcqs.explanation: The core advantage is reliability — a graph traversal doesn't depend on someone remembering to mention a dependency, unlike informal asking, which is exactly the failure mode lineage is meant to close. Lineage doesn't guarantee a change is safe (it just tells you who to check), it complements rather than replaces contracts, and informal asking is neither faster nor more complete in general — it's precisely the unreliable method lineage improves on.

mcqs.question: A dashboard shows a wrong number, and there are several transform steps between the raw source and the dashboard. How does lineage help find where the error was introduced?
options: It allows a direct backward traversal from the broken field through its immediate sources and their sources, narrowing down exactly which hop introduced the problem
It automatically fixes the bad number without further investigation
It only works if the error originated in the very first source table
It requires manually re-running every transform step to compare outputs
mcqs.explanation: Backward traversal is the specific mechanism — walking from the broken field to its direct sources, then theirs, isolates which hop actually introduced the discrepancy, turning a long manual search into a targeted graph walk. Lineage doesn't fix anything automatically, it works regardless of which hop the error originated at, and it doesn't require re-running transforms to compare outputs — that's a different debugging technique entirely.

mcqs.question: What's a key limitation of static SQL parsing as a method for capturing lineage?
options: It can miss dependencies expressed through dynamic SQL or queries built at runtime, which static analysis of the code can't fully follow
It requires the pipeline to actually execute before any lineage can be captured
It only works for pipelines written in Python, never SQL
It cannot capture lineage for more than one table at a time
mcqs.explanation: Static parsing reads code without running it, so any dependency that only becomes concrete at runtime — a dynamically constructed query, for instance — can slip past it, which is exactly the accuracy risk runtime tracking avoids by observing what actually happened. It's runtime tracking, not static parsing, that requires execution; static parsing works on SQL specifically (the opposite of being Python-only), and it isn't limited to one table at a time.

mcqs.question: A team maintains a hand-drawn lineage diagram in a wiki. Six months later, several pipelines have changed but the diagram hasn't been updated. What's the real danger here?
options: The diagram becomes completely blank and obviously unusable, so nobody would rely on it by mistake

The diagram still looks authoritative and gets trusted for impact analysis, even though it may now miss real dependencies or show ones that no longer exist, leading someone to ship an unsafe change believing it was checked
Wiki pages automatically detect and flag when their content is out of date
The diagram only affects new pipelines, not existing ones already in production
mcqs.explanation: The danger is specifically that the diagram doesn't announce its own staleness — it keeps looking authoritative while silently drifting from reality, so someone trusts it precisely when it can no longer be trusted. Wikis don't auto-detect staleness, a stale diagram doesn't go blank, and it can mislead investigations into any pipeline it claims to describe, new or old.
